title: Working with Dictionaries
objective: Add, change, and remove key-value pairs after a dictionary already exists.

sourceAlignment.title: Python Crash Course, 3rd Edition
sourceAlignment.author: Eric Matthes
sourceAlignment.note: Alignment metadata only. Lesson prose and exercises are original Code Forge material.

paragraphs: A dictionary isn't fixed once you create it. You can add a brand new key at any time just by assigning to it, even starting from an empty dictionary {}.
Assigning to a key that already exists doesn't add a duplicate — it overwrites the value that was there, which is how you update a dictionary as things change.
The del keyword removes a key-value pair permanently. Once it's deleted, looking up that key again raises a KeyError.
explanation.rule: dictionary[key] = value adds or overwrites a pair; del dictionary[key] removes one.

examples.title: Leveling Up
examples.code:
smith = {}
smith["name"] = "Ada"
smith["level"] = 1

smith["level"] = 2
print(smith)

del smith["level"]
print(smith)
examples.note: Assigning to an existing key updates it in place; del removes the pair entirely.

checks.question: Starting from forge = {"hp": 10}, what does forge["hp"] = 15 do?
options: Raises an error because "hp" already exists.

feedback.correct: Correct — assigning to an existing key overwrites its value.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite — a dictionary can only hold one value per key, so this overwrites it.

assignment.title: Durability Tracker
assignment.brief: Write repair(amount) that starts with item = {"durability": 50}, adds amount to item["durability"], then prints the dictionary.
requirements: Update item["durability"] by adding amount to it.
assignment.testHarness:
# ---- Code Forge validation ----
import io, contextlib
_cf_buf = io.StringIO()
with contextlib.redirect_stdout(_cf_buf):
    repair(25)
_cf_result = _cf_buf.getvalue()
print("__CF_TEST_OUTPUT__")
print(repr(_cf_result))

hints: You can update a dictionary value the same way you'd update a variable: item["durability"] += amount.
+= adds to the existing value and stores the result back.
Print item itself, not just the number — a dict prints as {'durability': 75}.
